evidence.claim: A CNAS commentary states that the average DoD supply chain spans five to six tiers and that DoD visibility is lost beyond tier two, with prime contractors also generally lacking visibility beyond direct suppliers.

The CNAS commentary argues that defense and dual-use startup capital has largely flowed to would-be tier-one companies while subtier suppliers remain exposed to uneven demand signals and appropriations.
The CNAS commentary says Congress could support vulnerable lower-tier suppliers by attaching requirements that appropriations be passed directly down to suppliers.

A third-party ForcedAlpha casefile identifies defense infrared optics and Western chalcogenide glass as a potential NDAA-driven bottleneck and names LightPath Technologies as one public supplier to verify in later layers.
evidence.source_title: The Optics Cliff — NDAA §834 and the Quiet Rebuild of Defense IR — ForcedAlpha Casefile

evidence.claim: A third-party ForcedAlpha casefile argues that qualified non-Chinese rare-earth magnet capacity may be materially smaller than headline capacity because feedstock origin and defense qualification matter.

memory_update.text: Politics theme should be treated as policy-created demand and regulatory chokepoints, not as a simple election basket.
Defense subtier supply-chain visibility is a high-priority node because DoD and primes may lack visibility beyond tier two while supply chains can span five to six tiers.
Rare-earth magnets and non-Chinese feedstock qualification are an underfollowed policy chokepoint to verify through NDAA text, DoD awards, and company filings.
Defense infrared optics and chalcogenide glass may be a narrow small-cap discovery lane if NDAA sourcing restrictions force prime requalification.
Domestic-content aerospace components are a plausible second-order beneficiary lane under tariff, Buy American, and defense sourcing pressure.
Later layers must verify each candidate with primary filings, contract awards, current policy text, customer evidence, capacity data, and market-pricing checks before any ranking survives.

layer1a.summary: Layer 1A decomposes the broad Politics theme into policy-driven chokepoints rather than headline election winners. The highest-quality funnel should focus on regulation-created demand, government spending pass-through, tariff and domestic-content reshoring, defense supply-chain fragility, and obscure qualified suppliers. The best discovery lanes are likely below the prime-contractor layer: specialty materials, compliant components, testing/certification, defense optics, rare-earth magnets, lower-tier aerospace suppliers, procurement software/data, and subcontractors exposed to appropriations flow-through. This is research support only and does not provide trading recommendations.

theme_map.public_market_search_strategy: Run a two-lane funnel. Use major defense primes, aerospace OEMs, and policy-sensitive megacaps only as reference demand indicators. The main alpha-discovery lane should map regulatory deadlines and procurement flows into obscure public suppliers with narrow products, low analyst mindshare, small or mid-cap market values, customer concentration, and hidden compliance leverage. Search across SEC filings, DoD contract awards, NDAA text, earnings-call transcripts, backlog disclosures, customer concentration notes, tariff-exposure disclosures, Buy American compliance language, and supplier-certification announcements. Prioritize companies where politics changes customer qualification or scarcity economics, not merely companies with high-level exposure to government revenue.
supply_side_constraints: Defense supply chains can span five to six tiers while visibility often degrades beyond tier two, creating hidden fragility in subtier suppliers
Small lower-tier defense suppliers may face uneven demand signals and appropriations timing even when prime contractors receive large awards
Qualified non-Chinese or allied-source rare-earth and magnet supply appears narrower than headline mine or factory capacity suggests
Specialty defense optical materials and chalcogenide glass capacity may face qualification and statutory-compliance constraints
Aerospace and defense suppliers exposed to domestic raw-material documentation may face reshoring, quality, OSHA, and on-time-delivery scrutiny
Certification, requalification, and customer audit cycles can create bottlenecks even where nominal capacity exists
